question.text: A photon of energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10.2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal"> </mi><mi>eV</mi></math> corresponds to light of wavelength <math><msub><mrow><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math> Due to an electron transition from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in a hydrogen atom, the light of wavelength <math><mi>λ</mi></math> is emitted. If we take into account the recoil of the atom when the photon is emitted, then

solution.text:
Without recoil of the atom, the entire energy is carried away by the photon.

hcλ0=10.2 eV

With recoil of the atom, energy is shared between photon and atom. So, the energy of the photon is less, hence its wavelength is more.

hcλ<hcλ0

∴λ0<λ
